Underfront — General Lore

> **Name:** the game is called **"Underfront"** (*ქვესკნელის ფრონტი*): the gates of the underworld have opened all over the world, and every nation
> fights the evil of its own mythology in the trenches. The main trench — **Ambri's Furrow** — is the furrow that Ambri ploughed with his foot
> on the way to his grave (`02-chronology.md`).

> Working version. Dates and details may change. This is the general frame of the world;
> detailed stories (letters, reports, tales) are written in separate files.

---

## Prologue

> "My father used to say that the earth keeps the dead. He never said that the earth gives them back."
>
> — a letter found in the pocket of a Colchian levyman. Author unknown.

---

## History in Three Ages

The history of this world is made up of three ages (details — `02-chronology.md`):
1. **The Rise (1825–1870)** — the century of steam, the opening of the gates, the coalition of nations, the knowledge of the gods, the giants and **the Age of Sealing**,
   when the gates are closed one after another. In 1870 the coalition declares the war over.
2. **The Great Catastrophe (1871–1872)** — **the Night of Opening**: the Listeners, traitors hidden inside the coalition, open every seal
   from the inside on a single night. The coalition falls apart, and that same spring the Lesser Caucasus breaks open. The war is stopped only by **Ambri's sacrifice**.
3. **The Endless War (1872–...)** — a ring of trenches around the Wound, generations in the trenches, the Grand Harness. A war with no end in sight.

## 1. The Old Seals

Every nation remembers its old enemy.

The Greeks remember Cronus and the Titans, locked away in Tartarus. The Northerners remember Fenrir, bound with a chain.
The Georgians remember the devis, whom Kopala drove under the earth with lightning. The Egyptians remember Apep, whom the sun barque fights every night.

People thought these were fairy tales.

They were not fairy tales. They were **seals** — the chains, locks and graves left by gods and heroes, which
held back the evil hidden beneath every land. Every mythology has its own underworld, and every underworld is real.

One of them — **Hell** — is a kingdom of the underworld with its own capital, **Pandemonium**, and its own
armies, which have waited for centuries.

## 2. The Century of Steam and the Breaking of the Seals

In the first half of the 19th century, with the coming of the steam engine, people began to dig into the earth as never before.

Railways cut through mountains. Mines went deeper than ever. Archaeologists opened old barrows and caves.
Steam engines worked day and night, and the earth shook.

The seals cracked. And for some, that was no accident.

**The Listeners** — a secret brotherhood of heretics of every nation, which for centuries had listened to the voices coming from below —
knew exactly where to dig. In the name of foreign companies they opened mines wherever there were seals. At the foot of the Lesser Caucasus
they dug the **Black Shaft**, and the Colchian mountain wardens — the last faithful keepers of the old oath — fought it in vain.

The **workers** noticed it first: in the deep shafts they heard voices, the walls grew warm, and some miners did not come back.
Some came back — different. They whispered that someone below had spoken to them and offered them power.

Then the **gates** opened.

## 3. The Gates

The gates did not open in one night, nor in one place. They opened over decades — small rifts
in fields, in mines, on the beds of lakes, in old castles.

From every land rose **the evil of its own mythology**:

- from the land of Greece — the spawn of the Titans;
- from the land of the North — the jötnar and Fenrir's wolves;
- from the Slavic lands — the zmei and Koschei's servants;
- from the Celtic isles — the Fomorians;
- from the Egyptian desert — Apep's serpents;
- from the land of Georgia — the **devis**.

Every nation faced its old enemy. And wherever a gate opened, **the legions of Hell** rose from it too —
in orderly ranks, with ranks and orders, as if marching to a war planned long ago.

## 4. The Heretics

The most terrible thing was that **people** joined the underworld too.

In every country there were those who went over to the dark side: miners who were offered power below; soldiers
who no longer believed in their officers; peasants who had nothing to lose; the rich who wanted
more. Many had a just grievance. The underworld offered them all one thing — **power** — and that power changed them all.

They were called **heretics**. They serve the dark power of their own land, consecrate their weapons with blood, and in the trenches
fight their own people.

**No country has fallen.** But not one country remains whose sons do not stand on both sides of the trench.
Brother fights brother, and, so they say, they often recognise each other.

## 5. The Great Breakthrough and Ambri's Sacrifice

The greatest gate opened **in the mountains of the Lesser Caucasus**.

The earth split open with a roar, and out of it rose the **Father of Devis** — an ancient, many-headed devi whose heads grow back
as soon as they are cut off. The legions of Hell followed him. The front almost broke. Colchis and Iberia stood on the edge of collapse.

Then **Ambri** came.

Ambri, the giant of the old epic — the one whose strength was such that even dead he defeated Amirani. In the epic the dead Ambri
is carried on a cart, and Amirani cannot lift his foot where it hangs from the cart — "the dead defeated the living". Our
legend adds: Ambri never fully died — for centuries he slept in his barrow. The Colchians dug open the barrow
and woke the giant, and Ambri lay down in the rift of his own will. The cart, as in one version of the epic, was drawn by **twelve yoke of oxen**
— steam oxen now. On the way his foot, hanging from the cart, ploughed the earth like a plough — and that furrow is still
the front's **main trench**.

Ambri was buried alive in the gate. With his huge body he sealed the door of the underworld and left the Father of Devis below.

Ambri died. But, as in the old epic, **even dead, Ambri is strong** — his body holds the seal to this day.

The place where Ambri was buried is called **the Wound** — a great crater in the heart of the mountains, where no nation lives any more.

## 6. Khvamli — the Key

Ambri's body is **the lock**. But every lock has **a key**.

In the caves of Mount Khvamli, together with the old treasure of the Georgian kings, are kept **Amirani's chains** — the chains with which
the gods chained the titan to the Caucasus. When the smiths of Iberia freed Amirani, the chains were taken to Khvamli. They are
the only thing that can open Ambri's seal — the old rivalry of Ambri and Amirani binds their powers together.

That is why the **good gods** stand on Khvamli and guard the chains. They are bound there by their own oath — and that is exactly
why **they cannot help the people at the front**.

The people in the trenches are alone.

## 7. The Knowledge of the Gods: Giants, Steam and Alchemy

The gods could not come, but they left their **knowledge**.

Every nation has a smith god — Shavkhan, Hephaestus, Svarog, Ilmarinen, Goibniu. With their knowledge people built
steam weapons, armour, prosthetics and **giants** — the colossi of national myth that lead the troops at the front.

They also learned **alchemy**: dead water, which closes wounds; living water, which brings the dead back to life;
dragon's teeth, which are sown in the earth and spring up as warriors. But alchemy always has a price.

The underworld has its own alchemy too — and it is far more terrible.

## 8. The Grand Harness

The heretics know that to break the seal they need two things: the chains of Khvamli and blood on Ambri's grave.

For this they built **the Grand Harness** (დიდი უღელი) — a steam-driven walking fortress-city.

The Grand Harness is driven by steam engines and dragged by **devis and captive giants yoked in harness**. It is the mirror image of Ambri's twelve
oxen: the light side brought Ambri to his grave in a yoke — the heretics drag their city toward his grave with
captives.

On the city's back stands a stepped **altar**. Blood flows from it through the city's belly into the engines — the city runs on blood
too. Aboard the city are the headquarters of Hell's front general, **Beelzebub**, the heretics' factories and the captives' cages.

The Grand Harness walks around the Wound. When it stands over Ambri's grave and enough blood is spilled on the altar,
the seal will break.

**The light side's main task: do not let the Grand Harness reach the grave.**

## 9. Why People Are Still Alive — the Dark Side's Civil War

> "If they came at us together, we would be finished in a week. Our only ally is their hatred for each other."
>
> — Spasalari Nino's report to the king

The dark side is strong — far stronger on the surface. But **it is not united**, and that alone is why humankind still lives.

- **Hell and the other underworlds** are enemies of one another. Hell wants to conquer the surface for itself. The devis, the Titans,
  the jötnar and the other old evils want to submit to no one. Where the legions and the old monsters rise in the same place,
  they often fight each other first.
- **The old evils fight each other too.** The spawn of Cronus have nothing in common with Fenrir's wolves. Every underworld
  wants its own land.
- **The legions and the heretics** fight together, but they do not trust each other. The legions call the heretics "material".
  The heretics call the legions "the new masters". They often shoot each other in the back.
- **The dark side's leaders have different plans for the seal.** Beelzebub wants the Father of Devis to become Hell's captive.
  The heretics' leader, the Harness-Lord, wants the Father of Devis to break every seal, Hell's included. And the Bakbak-Devi, yoked in the Grand Harness,
  waits for the day it can take revenge on both.

In No Man's Land it often happens that a light-side squad reaches the site of a battle and finds only dead heretics and legionnaires
who have killed each other. The soldiers call this **"a gift from the gods"** — the only gift they will ever get from Khvamli.

## 10. The Front — 1914

In 1914 the front is a **ring** around the Wound. The trench war has gone on for more than forty years — most soldiers have never seen peace.

- **To the north** the trenches are held by **Colchis** and **Iberia**.
- **To the south and east** — the neighbouring peoples: **the Armenian Highlands** and **the Oghuz Lands**, who are also fighting their own old enemies (see `08-southern-eastern-allies.md`).
- **Inside the Wound** — the host of the underworld, the legions of Hell and the heretics of every nation.

Wherever the Grand Harness goes, the front goes too — and there is the bloodiest fighting.

Between the trenches lies **No Man's Land** — with ditches, barbed wire, the bones of slain monsters and the great furrow
ploughed by Ambri's foot. Small squads fight here: they scout, take captives, search for relics, hunt monsters and try
to cut the Grand Harness's path — or open it. The eight zones of the strip and its rules — `../rules/no-mans-land.md`.

## 11. The Sides

### The Light Side — the Coalition of Nations
Each nation with its own army, the legend of its own patron gods and its own giant.

- **Colchis** — bronze, fire, oxen and the sea. Knights with sword and shield, a levy with rifles, bronze fire-breathing
  bull-tanks, the alchemy of the Sisters of Medea. Giant — **the Dragon of the Fleece**.
- **Iberia** — iron, lightning, mountains and dogs. Khevsur warriors in chain shirts, Tush riders and shepherds with nagazi,
  Thunderbolt Gunners, walking fortress-towers. Giant — **the Colossus of Armazi**, the bronze statue-titan of the supreme god. Beside them fights **Amirani**, the living titan-hero, with his hound Qursha.

- **The Ring Battalion** — the tribute army: squads of every nation in one battalion, with forty tongues. It takes allies with no mark-up;
  its orders are carried by interpreters. Giant — **the Colossus of the Sea Gate**.

### The Dark Side
- **The Infernal Legions** — a disciplined war machine from Pandemonium. Ranks, legions, volleys and formations.
  The commander-in-chief is **Baal**, the front's general — **Beelzebub**. Giant — **the Behemoth**.
- **The Grand Harness** — heretics and creatures of the underworld: maddened rebels, kudiani, kaji, devis,
  gveleshapi. Leader — **the Elder of the Defiant**. Giant — **the Bakbak-Devi**.
- **The Brotherhood of Listeners** — the secret brotherhood of every nation that built the seals and opened them: the planted, sabotage, locks.
  Giant — **the Gifted Colossus**.
- **Kajeti** — the sorcerous smiths of folklore: cast-iron soldiers, stitched bodies, walking furnaces. The kaji sell to everyone and
  see everything as material. Giant — **the Citadel-Colossus of Kajeti**.

---

lore:02-chronology.en:
Chronology: from the Seals to the Trenches

> Working version. Alternative history.
> In this world there was no world war between nations. "The Great War" is the war of the surface against the underworld.

---

## Three Ages

The history of the war divides into three parts:
1. **The Rise** — humankind unites, receives the knowledge of the gods and closes the gates one after another. The war is almost won.
2. **The Great Catastrophe** — at the victory celebration everything collapses: betrayal from within, gates thrown open, the great breakthrough.
3. **The Endless War** — the front stalls in the trenches, and the war passes from generation to generation.

---

# Preface — the Old Time

## I. The Age of Myths — the Seals

> "In the beginning the earth was open, and whatever lived below came up whenever it pleased."
>
> — a mountain tale, recorded in Khevsureti

In a time older than human memory every land had its own evil and every nation its own protector.

The gods of the Greeks locked Cronus and the Titans in Tartarus. The gods of the Northerners bound Fenrir with a chain.
Egypt's sun barque fought Apep every night. And in the mountains of Colchis and Iberia stood Kopala — he drove the devis under the earth
with lightning, and the oldest and mightiest of them, **the Father of Devis**, he buried deepest of all, beneath **the Lesser Caucasus**.

So the **seals** were made: chains, locks and graves that held back the evil hidden beneath every land.

Among all the underworlds there was one that did not rage or roar. **Hell** waited. In its capital,
**Pandemonium**, the legions divided into ranks, entered themselves on lists and began what no one else in the underworld did — **planning**.

## II. The Age of Heroes — Amirani and Ambri

> "When Ambri died, Amirani laughed. Ambri put a hand out of the grave, and Amirani stopped laughing."
>
> — a fragment of the epic

After the gods came the heroes.

**Amirani**, the titan-hero, gave people iron. For this the gods chained him to the Caucasus and left his faithful hound
**Qursha** beside him.

**Ambri** was a giant whose strength knew no limit. Even dead he defeated Amirani: Ambri's body was being carried by cart
to the burial place, and Amirani could not lift his foot where it hung from the cart. In one version of the epic the cart was drawn by twelve
yoke of oxen and buffalo; our chronicle says that on the way this foot ploughed the earth like a plough.

The epic says that even dead, Ambri is strong. The epic does not say the most important thing: **Ambri did not die**. He fell asleep in his barrow —
and slept for thousands of years.

## III. The Centuries of the Wardens

> "We guard. What we guard, we no longer remember. But we guard."
>
> — the words of an Iberian border guard, from an old chronicle

On both sides of the Lesser Caucasus two kingdoms arose — **Colchis** in the west and **Iberia** in the east. Both swore one
and the same oath: **nothing beneath the earth must be let out.**

Colchis kept the **Golden Fleece** in its royal house and set beside it a **dragon** that never slept.
The kings of both kingdoms hid their treasure in the caves of **Mount Khvamli**.

Centuries passed. Sometimes, once in several generations, a cold winter came to the mountains, the earth shook at night and in the villages
people told of having seen a devi. The mountain warriors took up arms and went up into the mountains, and some did not come back. People called these
**"devi winters"** and put them in fairy tales.

Over time the reason for the oath was forgotten. The oath became a custom, the custom a fairy tale, the fairy tale a fright for children.

## IV. The Age of Whispers (16th–18th centuries)

> "I didn't summon him. He came by himself and asked me what I wanted. To tell the truth, I'd been waiting a long time for someone to ask."
>
> — a heretic's confession, from an interrogation record

Hell could not rise. But it could **speak**.

In the cities of Europe scholars and alchemists worked alone at night, and some of them heard a voice in the silence. The voice offered knowledge,
power, glory — and always a contract. So appeared the first who signed with **Mephistopheles**.

In this age the books were written that were later called **grimoires**. People took them for books of witchcraft. In truth
they were **intelligence reports** — lists of Hell's ranks, legions and generals, written down by those who were spoken to
from below. No one realised that this was **a muster-roll**.

In every nation, quietly, **secret brotherhoods** appeared. They did not know each other, but they all prayed in one language — the language
they had learned from below.

At the end of the 18th century the brotherhoods found each other and united. The new brotherhood was called **the Listeners** — because they
listened to the voices from below. The Listeners included people of every nation and belonged to none. The voices told them
what everyone on the surface had forgotten: **where the greatest seal is** — beneath the Lesser Caucasus. And in the valleys of the Caucasus, on the old land of Kajeti, the **kaji** — the sorcerous smiths — relit
their forges.

---

# Part One — the Rise (1825–1870)

## V. Steam and Cracks (1825–1847)

> "The shaft is deeper than on the map. Every morning we measure it, and every morning it is deeper."
>
> — the diary of an engineer at the Black Shaft, 1840

The steam engine changed everything.

People began to dig into the earth as never before. Railways cut through mountains. Mines went deeper than ever.
Archaeologists opened old barrows. Engines droned day and night, and the earth shook.

**In 1838** a foreign mining company appeared at the foot of the Lesser Caucasus. It had a great deal of money, spoke many languages and
said it was looking for copper. In truth it was **the Listeners**, and they were looking for the seal. So the **Black Shaft** was opened —
the deepest mine ever dug. Workers were brought in from every side; they did not know for whom they were digging.

The Colchian mountain wardens — the last faithful keepers of the old oath — did not like the shaft. No one remembered the reason for the oath, but they
remembered the oath: **nothing beneath the earth must be let out.** They demanded that the shaft be closed. The company answered with money, then with threats.

**In 1841** workers began to disappear in the Black Shaft. Some came back after a few days — pale, silent, different.
They said someone below had spoken to them, and that he had a gift for them.

**In 1844** Colchian wardens went down the shaft at night to see what was being dug. One came back. He said that at the bottom of the shaft
the Listeners were not digging through a wall — **they were opening a seal**.

The seals cracked. All over the world — wherever the Listeners dug.

## VI. The War of the Gates and the Coalition (1847–1860)

> "We expected beasts. An army came."
>
> — a Colchian officer's report, 1849

**In 1847** the first **gates** opened — not in one place and not in one night, but over years, in fields,
in mines, on the beds of lakes, in old castles. From every land rose **the evil of its own mythology**: the spawn of the Titans,
the jötnar, the zmei, the Fomorians, Apep's serpents — and in the Caucasus, **the devis**.

**In 1849** the **legions** of Hell appeared. They did not fight like beasts. They had banners, ranks, orders and
supply lines. The readers of the old grimoires were horrified: the lists were accurate.

**In 1852** the Listeners and their secret brotherhoods rose at once — in hundreds of cities, in dozens of countries. This year is called **the Year of Revolt**.
For the first time the heretics fought openly, against their own people. **No country fell** — but not one country
remained whose sons did not stand on both sides.

**In 1855** nations that had had nothing in common swore **the Coalition Oath**.

**In 1858** the good gods gave people their last gift — **the knowledge of the forge**. With the knowledge of Shavkhan, Hephaestus, Svarog,
Ilmarinen and the other smith gods, people built steam weapons, armour, prosthetics and the first **giants**.
They also learned **alchemy** — dead water, living water, dragon's teeth.

**In 1859**, at the Colchian Sea Gate, **the Dragon of the Fleece** — the first giant — drove the gveleshapi back into the sea. The nations saw
that the knowledge of the gods worked, and every one of them began building a giant of its own.

## VI-a. The Age of Sealing (1860–1870)

> "We know how a door is shut. First the giant, then the smith, then the alchemist. And then silence."
>
> — from the coalition's engineering manual, 1864

This was humankind's **golden decade**.

The coalition armies learned to **close** the gates. A giant drove the monsters back and pushed the legions back into the earth, and the smiths
forged a new seal on the gate — of iron, of bronze, consecrated with alchemy. The seals were built by **the coalition's engineers**, from every
nation, and everyone trusted them.

One after another the gates closed. The Greeks' **Talos** barred the Titans' gate. The Northerners' giant drove the jötnar back into
the mountains. In the mountains of Colchis and Iberia the devis became fairy tales again.

Cities were rebuilt. Railways were laid again. The steam factories began to work for peace instead of war.

**In 1868** the last known gate was closed.

**In the autumn of 1870**, at the Colchian **Sea Gate** — where the first giant had fought — every nation of the coalition gathered
for **the Victory Celebration**. The giants stood in the harbour, banners flew, and the coalition declared: **the war is over**.

The armies went home. The giants were returned to the factories. The smiths hung their swords up in the sheds.

Very few did not laugh at the celebration.

---

# Part Two — the Great Catastrophe (1871–1872)

## VII. The Night of Opening and the Great Breakthrough (1871–1872)

> "The mountain smiled. That's what I told my officer. He told me mountains don't smile. Then the mountain opened its mouth."
>
> — an Iberian border guard, 1871

**One night in the spring of 1871** — this night is called **the Night of Opening** — hundreds of sealed gates opened at once all over the world.

The seals did not break. They were **opened** — from the inside.

**The Listeners** had hidden inside the coalition for twenty years: as officers, engineers, smiths, writers. It was they who had built
many of the seals — and in every seal they had left a hidden **lock**. After the celebration, when the armies had gone home, the Listeners
opened every lock in a single night.

By morning every nation had its own gate open again — and no army. The coalition fell apart: every nation called its army
home to defend its own land. Some nations accused each other of betrayal, because the traitors had been in everyone's ranks.

And that same spring the Lesser Caucasus broke open.

This was no small rift. It was **the greatest gate** ever opened. Out of it rose **the Father of Devis** — many-headed,
as tall as a mountain, and in place of every head cut off a new one grew. Behind him rose the legions of Hell, in ranks, with banners.

By summer Colchis and Iberia were on the edge of collapse — **alone**, because every other nation was fighting its own gates.

**In the autumn** the smiths of Iberia did what no one had dared for thousands of years — they climbed the Caucasus and
**freed Amirani**. The titan put on armour forged by the smiths of Shavkhan and went into battle with Qursha. He fought the Father of Devis
for weeks. But every head Amirani cut off grew back.

**In the winter** Amirani's chains were taken to **Khvamli**, to the old treasure of the kings. It was then discovered that these chains, which had once
held the titan captive, are the only thing that can both open and close the seal of the underworld. Ambri and Amirani were old rivals,
and their powers belonged to each other.

**The good gods** swore an oath on Khvamli to guard the chains. Bound by that oath, they could never again help the front.

The people were left alone.

**In the spring of 1872** the Colchians dug open **Ambri's barrow**.

The giant was asleep. He woke, listened and — just as in the epic — **twelve yoke of oxen** carried him to his burial place. Only these
oxen were steam ones, of bronze and iron, and the burial place was the gate. Ambri's foot, fallen from the cart, ploughed the earth and left a furrow
that is today **the main trench**.

Ambri lay down in the gate of his own will. With his huge body he sealed the door of the underworld. The Father of Devis remained below.

This day is called **the Day of Ambri's Burial**. In Colchis and Iberia every year, on this day, every soldier stands up and falls silent.

Where the gate had been, a crater remained — **the Wound**. Ambri's body is the **lock** of the seal. The chains of Khvamli are **the key**.

---

# Part Three — the Endless War (1872–...)

## VIII. The War of the Ring (1872–1913)

> "My grandfather dug this trench. My father died in it. I live in it."
>
> — a letter from a Colchian levyman, 1910

Around the Wound a **ring of trenches** appeared: Colchis and Iberia to the north, the armies of the neighbouring nations to the south and east.
The furrow ploughed by Ambri's foot grew deeper and wider and became the backbone of the front. Children were born and grew up in the trenches.

**In 1875**, under **the Sea Gate Agreement**, the nations took on **the Ring Tribute**: every nation sends one squad to the Wound each year.
The coalition no longer exists, but the Wound is everyone's common front (see `06-european-allies.md`).

**In 1880**, interrogating a captured heretic, the light side learned for the first time what the enemy needs to break the seal:
**the chains of Khvamli** and **blood on Ambri's grave**.

**In 1884** the heretics attempted a march on Khvamli. Two hundred went. No one came back, and no one knows their fate.
Since then no one has dared to march on Khvamli. The chains keep up Amirani's old custom: **once a year, on one night in spring**,
every smith in both kingdoms strikes the anvil with a hammer — so that the chain does not wear thin. And the cave of Khvamli, by the old tradition, opens **once
every seven years** (1891, 1898, 1905, 1912). At every opening the border guards watch the mountain. In 1905 one of them said that someone came out.

**In 1889**, inside the Wound, construction of **the Grand Harness** began. Its architect was **Mulciber**; its engineers were the fallen
**"Watchers"**, Azazel and Gadreel, who taught the heretics metallurgy and the art of weapons. For ten years
heretics and captives built a city that was meant to move.

**In 1899** — **the First March of the Grand Harness.** The devis and captive giants yoked in harness moved the city for the first time. On its back
stood the altar, and blood flowed down into the engines. For the first time, the front moved.

**In 1904** the light side stopped the Grand Harness for the first time. **The Dragon of the Fleece** and **Amirani** together fought the **Bakbak-Devi**,
which was yoked at the head of the Harness. The city fell back. The site of that battle is called **the Dragon's Field** today.

**In 1907** **Beelzebub** — Hell's front general — arrived at the front and set up his headquarters on the Grand Harness. Since then the legions
have fought differently: more orderly, more patiently, more to a plan.

**In the winter of 1913** the Grand Harness stopped for several months. Scouts brought word that it had been **rebuilt**: heavier chains,
new engines, a bigger altar.

## IX. 1914 — the Present

> "It's moving again. This time it's coming straight on."
>
> — the last entry in a lost scout's notebook

**In the spring of 1914** the Grand Harness set off — this time straight for **Ambri's grave**.

Captives are sacrificed on the altar every day. The heretics need more blood, so there are raids in No Man's Land every night.
The front moves wherever the Harness goes.

In the trenches stand soldiers who have never seen peace. Their grandfathers saw Ambri's burial. Their fathers fought on the Dragon's
Field. Now it is their turn.

**This is where the game begins.**

Named Battles (1847–1913)

> Working version. Every place and battle is invented.
> The same battle often has two names — one from the light side, the other from the heretics. Neither version is equally reliable.
> At the end of each battle there is a **scenario idea** for the tabletop game.

---

## 1. The Sealing of the Black Shaft — 1847

> "Singing came up out of the shaft. They sang in many languages — in the voices of the workers who had been taken down. We blew it anyway."
>
> — the memoir of a Colchian mountain warden

**Sides:** the Colchian mountain wardens and smiths — the brotherhood of **the Listeners**, the workers they had changed, and the first devis.

The Black Shaft was dug by **the Listeners** — the secret brotherhood of heretics of every nation, which knew where the seal was. The Colchian wardens
had tried for years to close it and failed.

When the seal broke at the bottom of the Black Shaft in 1847, the Listeners turned the mouth of the shaft into a stronghold. The changed workers
came up from the depths — armed this time, and behind them the first devis.

The Colchian wardens stormed the mouth of the shaft for three days and nights. On the third night the smiths lowered explosives into the shaft and
brought it down — with everyone below: the Listeners, the devis, and the workers who might perhaps still have been saved.

**Outcome:** the shaft was closed. The gate never opened in this place again. The Listeners' leaders escaped.
**Legacy:** from this battle was born the fighting order of **the Smiths of Shavkhan** — smiths who not only forge, but also destroy.
**The heretics call it:** "the First Betrayal".

**Scenario idea:** the light side holds the mouth of the shaft and must bring up the explosives; the dark side comes up from below in waves.

---

## 2. The Night of the Third Bridge — 1852

> "He called my name. I knew the voice. It was my brother. I fired."
>
> — an Iberian soldier's testimony, from a court-martial

**Sides:** the garrison of an Iberian town — members of the same town's secret brotherhood.

**In the Year of Revolt** the heretics rose in hundreds of cities at once. In one of Iberia's market towns, built on three river
bridges, the revolt began at midnight. The heretics took the first two bridges. The garrison made its stand on the third bridge
and fought until dawn.

It was the first battle in which soldiers recognised their neighbours, relatives and brothers in the enemy's ranks.

**Outcome:** the town remained in the light side's hands, but half of it burned.
**Legacy:** after this night a custom arose at the front — a heretic is not addressed by name. The name no longer belongs to him.
**The heretics call it:** "the Night of Awakening".

**Scenario idea:** a town battle over three bridges; both sides are natives of the same town — players may use a "recognition" rule.

---

## 3. The Battle of the Sea Gate — 1859

> "The dragon opened its eye. Whether it had slept two thousand years or not, I don't know. But it knew exactly whom to fight."
>
> — a Colchian smith's diary

**Sides:** Colchis and **the Dragon of the Fleece** — gveleshapi risen from the sea and heretic sailors.

A year after the last gift of the gods, the smiths of Colchis finished their first giant: the old, never-sleeping
guardian dragon of the Fleece, rebuilt in bronze, iron and steam.

That same summer gveleshapi rose from the sea and attacked the Colchian harbour. The dragon went into battle for the first time.

**Outcome:** the harbour was saved. The gveleshapi went back into the sea.
**Legacy:** the first battle in which a **giant** fought. The nations saw that the knowledge of the gods worked — and began
building giants of their own.

**Scenario idea:** defending a harbour; a gveleshapi and heretic sailors come up out of the sea; the light side has a giant's support.

---

## 4. Qursha's Ravine — autumn 1871

> "Nine days. We stood for nine days. On the tenth day I looked round, and in the ravine there was only the dog. And Amirani."
>
> — the memoir of a Khevsur warrior

**Sides:** Iberia, Khevsur warriors, **Amirani** and **Qursha** — **the Father of Devis** and the legions of Hell.

In the autumn of the great breakthrough the smiths of Iberia freed Amirani. The first place he went into battle was a narrow
mountain ravine through which the legions were trying to get down into the Iberian lowlands.

The Khevsur warriors held the ravine for nine days while the people of the lowlands fled. Amirani fought the Father of Devis. He cut off head
after head — and every head grew back. On the tenth day Amirani fell back wounded. Qursha stayed in the ravine and covered his retreat.

**Outcome:** the people were saved. The ravine was lost.
**Legacy:** since then the ravine has been called **Qursha's Ravine**. It became clear that the Father of Devis cannot be killed — only locked away.
It was right after this battle that people began to think of Ambri.

**Scenario idea:** holding the ravine for a set number of rounds; the light side must endure, not win.

---

## 5. Ambri's March — spring 1872

> "The oxen roared with steam, the giant was silent, and all of us knew we were escorting him to his death."
>
> — a Colchian aznauri's letter

**Sides:** Colchis and Iberia together — the legions of Hell and the heretics.

After Ambri woke, twelve steam oxen had to carry him from the barrow to the gate — two days' journey, through the enemy's
lines. **Aznauri knights** and the **Monaspa** surrounded the cart. Iberia's warriors held the hills on both sides of the road.

The legions knew what was happening and threw everything into stopping it. Four of the twelve oxen died on the march.
Ambri's foot fell from the cart and ploughed the earth — and that furrow became a line of defence in which the escort took cover.

**Outcome:** Ambri reached the gate and lay down in it of his own will. The gate closed. **The Wound** began.
**Legacy:** this day is called **the Day of Ambri's Burial**. The furrow — **the main trench**. Some of the eight surviving oxen still
fight today — they are called **the Oxen of Ambri**.
**The heretics call it:** "the Great Theft" — the light side stole their victory.

**Scenario idea:** an escort mission — the light side escorts the cart from one edge of the table to the other.

---

## 6. The Forest of Bones — 1876

> "The ribs stood like trees. We fought among them, and both sides tried not to wake the owner of the bones."
>
> — the memoir of an Iberian thunderbolt gunner

**Sides:** Iberia — heretics and kudiani.

On the western rim of the Wound lay the skeleton of a huge creature of the underworld, killed during the great breakthrough. Its ribs stood
like a forest. The kudiani tried to bring it to life and make it a new gate.

For five weeks they fought among the ribs — close, with sword and knife, at night.

**Outcome:** the ritual failed. The skeleton remained in No Man's Land, belonging to neither side.
**Legacy:** the Forest of Bones is still the most dangerous place on the front. Relic hunters go there.

**Scenario idea:** a battle on dense terrain (the ribs); the dark side tries to complete a ritual in the centre of the table.

---

## 7. The Silence of Khvamli — 1884

> "They went up the mountain. We waited. The mountain said nothing."
>
> — an Iberian border guard's log

**Sides:** two hundred heretics — unknown.

This was not a battle anyone saw. Two hundred heretics, chosen from every nation, slipped quietly behind the front and set out
for Mount Khvamli to steal the chains.

They climbed Khvamli. No one came back. There was no gunfire and no screaming. The next morning there was snow on the mountain, and no tracks.

**Outcome:** unknown.
**Legacy:** no one dares march on Khvamli any more. At the front they say the gods are still there — and that they are merciless.

**What really happened (for the authors):** by the old tradition, Amirani's cave opens **once every seven years**, and every year the smiths
renew the chain — by striking the anvil with a hammer. The two hundred chose the very day of the opening. They went into the mountain and opened the kings' chest
**before its time** — against the chronicle's inscription: "whoever opens it before its time is a killer of kings". That same night the smiths of both kingdoms
struck their anvils, the chains grew strong, and the mountain closed. The gods did not kill them — the gods are bound by their oath. The two hundred remained inside
the mountain. At the opening of 1905 one came out, with a curse (`05-characters.md`, Armaz III). The next opening — **1919**.

**Scenario idea:** none. Khvamli is not a front. (A campaign legend; the 1919 opening — an idea for a future campaign.)

---

## 8. The Bloody Spring — 1899

> "The city was coming. Cities don't walk. This was coming."
>
> — a Colchian levyman's letter, his last

**Sides:** Colchis and Iberia — **the Grand Harness**, heretics, the legions of Hell.

**The First March of the Grand Harness.** After ten years of building, the heretics' city moved for the first time. The light side was not ready —
no one had believed it could move.

The devis and captive giants yoked in harness dragged the city across the front line. Wherever it passed, the trenches were levelled with the ground.
Captives were taken by the hundred — for the altar.

**Outcome:** the front fell back two kilometres. The bloodiest spring of the war.
**Legacy:** the light side understood that the Grand Harness is the war's main threat. Training began for squads that hunt giants and the Harness
— **the Huntresses of Dali** and **the Thunderbolt Gunners**.
**The heretics call it:** "the First Step".

**Scenario idea:** the light side falls back and tries not to leave any captives behind; the dark side gathers captives.

---

## 9. The Dragon's Field — 1904

> "The dragon bit the devi in the throat and did not let go. Amirani struck the Harness's chain with his hammer. Both fell together, and the city stopped."
>
> — the official report of the battle, Colchian headquarters

**Sides:** **the Dragon of the Fleece**, **Amirani**, Colchis and Iberia — **the Bakbak-Devi**, the Grand Harness.

For five years the Grand Harness wrecked the front. In 1904 the light side for the first time dared to stop it head-on.
Two giants went out together — the dragon from Colchis, Amirani from Iberia. Their target was the **Bakbak-Devi**, the mightiest devi, which
was yoked at the head of the Harness.

The dragon bit the devi in the throat and did not let go. Amirani broke the Harness's main chain. The Bakbak-Devi, wounded and half
free, fell back and dragged the city with it.

**Outcome:** the Grand Harness fell back. The dragon was badly damaged — the smiths spent three years restoring it.
**Legacy:** **the Dragon's Field** — the light side's greatest victory. A piece of the dragon's broken wing still lies on the field.

**Scenario idea:** small squads fight each other around the giants' battle — at risk of being trampled underfoot.

---

## 10. The Winter of Wire — 1907–1908

> "They did not come roaring. They came in step. Together. And the steam came ahead of them."
>
> — an Iberian officer's report

**Sides:** Colchis and Iberia — the legions of Hell under Beelzebub's command.

In the very first winter after Beelzebub's arrival, the legions changed the war. Their attacks were no longer chaotic. The legions cut the wire
at night, and in the morning released **underworld steam** — a poisonous alchemical cloud — down the wind,
and advanced behind it in line.

The light side did not yet know gas masks.

**Outcome:** Colchis lost a sector of the front. At the end of the winter Iberia's **Thunderbolt Gunners** scattered the cloud with lightning
and stopped the legions' line.
**Legacy:** both sides learned gas warfare. The light side gained gas masks and the antidotes of the Sisters of Medea.
Since then everyone knows that the legions fight **to a plan**.

**Scenario idea:** a gas cloud moves with the wind; the dark side advances in good order behind it.

---

## 11. The Night of the Sky-Ships — 1910

> "From above, the city looked alive. It was breathing. We dropped our bombs into its heart."
>
> — the memoir of a Colchian aviator

**Sides:** Colchis' **sky-ships** — the Grand Harness, blood balloons.

Colchis sent its sky-ships against the altar of the Grand Harness for the first time. On a moonlit night six zeppelins flew over
the Wound. The heretics' blood balloons rose to meet them.

**Outcome:** the altar was damaged. Two of the six ships came back.
**Legacy:** the Grand Harness stood still for four months while the altar was rebuilt. Since then the Harness always guards the sky.

**Scenario idea:** rescuing the crew of a downed ship in No Man's Land before the heretics take them captive.

---

## 12. The Raid of the Forty Scouts — winter 1913

> "Six of us came back. What we saw was worth forty lives. I hope."
>
> — a scout's report

**Sides:** the combined scouts of Colchis and Iberia — the garrison of the Grand Harness.

When the Grand Harness stopped in the winter of 1913, the light side sent forty scouts deep into the Wound — to find out what was happening.

Six came back. They brought word: the Harness has new, heavier chains, new engines and a bigger altar.
And a map of its new route — **straight to Ambri's grave**.

**Outcome:** the light side knows what is coming.
**Legacy:** the spring of 1914 — the start of the game.

**Scenario idea:** a night mission for silent scouts; the goal is to bring the information to the edge of the table, not to kill the enemy.

Characters

> Working version. All characters are invented (except the mythological heroes, who come from folklore).
> At the end of each story there is a **secret** — a plot kernel for future stories and campaigns.

---

# Colchis

## King Aeetes XIV

> "I was a child when Ambri went by. My father lifted me onto his shoulders so I could see. The giant turned toward me and smiled.
> For fifty-two years I have been trying to understand why."
>
> — the king's private diary

**Born:** 1862. **Reigning:** since 1889.

Aeetes XIV was ten years old on the day of Ambri's March. He sat on his father's shoulders as the twelve steam oxen passed the city gates, and
the giant — for the last time, before he lay down in the gate — looked over the crowd. To the child it seemed that Ambri was looking straight at him.

He came to the throne in 1889 — the year building began on the Grand Harness. His whole reign is a reign of war. He no longer goes
to the front — his health will not allow it — but for every fallen aznauri **he writes to the family himself**. One room of the palace
is filled entirely with copies of these letters. Over twenty-five years he has written thousands.

He is calm, speaks slowly and never shouts. His eristavis fear his silence.

**Secret:** the king is certain that Ambri said something to him that day — with his lips, without a sound. For forty-two years he has tried to
remember the word. He asked the Sisters of Medea to help him recover the memory with the cauldron. The sisters refused — for now.

**The truth (for the authors):** the word was **"lift"**. In the epic Amirani meets the dead Ambri on the road, on a cart: Ambri's foot
hangs from the cart, his mother asks Amirani to put the foot back on the cart — and Amirani cannot move it. "The dead defeated the living." The foot was lifted by Ambri's **sister**.
When Aeetes XIV remembers, he will think the word is about Amirani: when the seal weakens, the living must lift Ambri's burden. He is wrong
only by half — Amirani will try again and fail again. The burden will be lifted by **an ordinary person** — a woman, as in the epic. Who — is the secret of the final
campaign.

---

## Eristavi Zurab Bronze-Arm

> "I left my arm on the Dragon's Field. In return, this arm feels no pain."
>
> — Eristavi Zurab, to new recruits

**Born:** 1868. **Commander of the Colchian front:** since 1908.

Zurab is the son of a minor aznauri, from a family of mountain wardens — the family that fought at the sealing of the Black Shaft. He became a knight
in the Bloody Spring (1899), when the thirty men under his command brought twelve captives out from the foot of the altar of the
Grand Harness.

On the Dragon's Field (1904) he fought at the foot of the Dragon of the Fleece. When the Bakbak-Devi broke the dragon's wing, a shard of the wing cut off
Zurab's right arm. Master Eldar made him a **bronze steam arm** — from the same bronze as the dragon's wing.

Zurab is plain, loud, and lives in the trenches with his soldiers. He knows his soldiers by name. He **does not address heretics
by name** — but they say he himself remembers the name of everyone from his squad who went over to the dark side.

**Secret:** Zurab's younger brother was taken captive in 1899, in the Bloody Spring. Zurab believed he had been sacrificed on the altar.
One night in 1913 someone in No Man's Land called Zurab by his childhood nickname.

**The truth (for the authors):** the brother is **alive** — inside the Grand Harness, under a heretic's name. In 1899 he was in the cage of captives
that **Mzia** saved (`11-sacrifices.md`). In the epic Amirani cuts his way out of the swallowing monster from inside and strings a woven net between its ribs,
so that the sun, once it gets inside, will burn it. The brother too is "in the belly of the beast": he works at the Harness's engines and **weaves the net** — preparing
to let the fire in from inside one day. The call in 1913 was his. Zurab does not know whether he is loyal — and neither do the heretics.

---

## Mother-Healer Eliso

> "Death is a door. I know how to shut it. Each time it is a little harder."
>
> — Mother-Healer Eliso

**Born:** unknown. They say — before 1800.

Eliso is the eldest of **the Sisters of Medea** — the order of healing women that keeps the alchemy of Colchis. No one knows how old she is.
Her name appears in the old lists at the time of the sealing of the Black Shaft (1847) too — as the healer who treated the mountain wardens.

They say she has **climbed out of Medea's cauldron three times**. Each time she came out young — and each time she remembered a little less.
Today she looks like a woman of forty, but her eyes are very old.

Eliso is the only one who knows **where the sisters get the dragon's teeth**. She tells no one — not even the king.

She is stern, cold and very precise. The soldiers worship her and fear her.

**Secret:** the dragon's teeth are running out. Eliso used the real, ancient teeth of the Dragon of the Fleece years ago. What they have
now are **devi teeth** — from devis killed in No Man's Land. The warriors that spring from these teeth are stronger.
And they turn on each other more often.

---

## Master Eldar

> "Don't talk to the dragon as if it were a machine. It's listening to you."
>
> — Master Eldar, to his apprentices

**Born:** 1859 — the year the Dragon of the Fleece first fought (the Battle of the Sea Gate).

Eldar is chief of **the Smiths of Shavkhan** and chief mechanic of **the Dragon of the Fleece**. His grandfather was among the dragon's first builders,
his father among its mechanics. Eldar grew up in the dragon's belly, among its engines, and says he knows the dragon's voice better than his
own.

After the Dragon's Field (1904) the dragon was badly damaged. Eldar restored it over **three years** — and in those three years,
they say, he never came out of the dragon's belly. In the same period he made Eristavi Zurab's bronze arm and designed the engines of the new generation
of the Oxen of Ambri.

He speaks little, works a great deal, and his hands are always black.

**Secret:** while restoring the dragon, Eldar found in its old bronze heart something the smiths had not put there: **a scrap of golden fleece** —
a piece of the Golden Fleece. Eldar told no one. Since then, at night, when everyone is asleep, the dragon turns its head toward Khvamli.

---

# Iberia

## King Armaz III

> "My father died in the palace, writing a letter, when the gas came in through the window. I no longer live in the palace."
>
> — King Armaz III

**Born:** 1888. **Reigning:** since 1908.

Armaz III's father, King Armaz II, died in **the Winter of Wire** (1907–1908) — not at the front, but behind it, in his palace,
when the wind carried the legions' underworld steam twenty kilometres. The king was writing an order for the front.

The twenty-year-old son took the throne, and his first order **turned the palace into a hospital**. He moved to the front himself and has lived in the trenches ever since.
The mountain communities — who never trusted the lowland kings — respect him, because he wears a chain shirt and scouts with the Tush
and their nagazi.

He is young, bold and sometimes reckless. Spasalari Nino often has to pull him back.

**Secret:** the king is sure his father's death was no accident — that the wind did not change by itself. The legions of **Andras**
sow discord. Armaz is searching for a traitor in Iberia's council. He has not found one yet.

**The truth (for the authors):** the wind did not change by itself. That night the order to open the palace windows was given **in the king's voice** — it was a
Listeners' **Voice-Master**. He was brought into the palace by a man who **came out of Khvamli** in 1905 — one of the two hundred (`03-named-battles.md`, No. 7).
According to the chronicle, the kings' chest on Khvamli bears the inscription: "whoever opens it before its time is a killer of kings". The two hundred opened the chest before
its time. The one who came out carries that curse — and he is now in Iberia's council, under another name.

---

## Spasalari Nino Thunder-Eye

> "The cloud came on the wind. We could not change the wind. So we burned the cloud."
>
> — Spasalari Nino's report, 1908

**Born:** 1874. **Commander-in-chief of Iberia:** since 1908.

Nino is the daughter of a Pshav smith. She was in love with lightning from childhood — they say that at ten she "caught" a thunderbolt in a storm
with an iron rod and lost her left eye. Now she has a **bronze lens** there, in which a blue spark turns. That is where her nickname comes from.

She was the first commander of **the Thunderbolt Gunners** — and the first to test a steam-electric rifle on a monster. In **the Winter of Wire**
(1908), when the legions' gas cloud covered the Iberian lines, Nino lined the Thunderbolt Gunners up in front of the cloud and fired lightning into it.
The cloud caught fire and burned away. The legions' line advancing behind it was caught in the fire.

After that the new king made her spasalari.

She is calm, precise and merciless. She believes the war will be won by engines — not by heroism.

**Secret:** Nino is working on a weapon that fires a **giant**-sized bolt of lightning — enough to stop the engines of the Grand Harness
with a single strike. The problem is that energy like that has only one source: **Amirani's armour**, which is filled with lightning from inside.

---

## Amirani and Qursha

> "I gave people iron, and for that they chained me. Now people have taken off my chain and given me iron. I am in their debt."
>
> — Amirani, to the Thunderbolt Gunners

**Titan-hero.** From folklore.

In the old epic Amirani gave people iron, and the gods chained him to the Caucasus — together with his faithful hound, **Qursha**.
He hung there for thousands of years.

In the autumn of 1871 the smiths of Iberia climbed the mountain and freed him. **The Smiths of Shavkhan** made the titan iron armour
with lightning coils inside. That same week Amirani went down into **Qursha's Ravine** and fought the Father of Devis for nine days. He was defeated. He does not forget it.

**Qursha** — half dog, half something older — stayed in the ravine and covered Amirani's retreat. Everyone thought he had died.
Three days later he came back, covered in wounds, with a devi's head in his jaws.

Since 1872 Amirani has stood beside **Ambri's grave** and leaves it only when the Grand Harness comes near. On the Dragon's Field (1904)
he fought beside the Dragon of the Fleece and broke the Harness's main chain.

Amirani speaks little. He looks at people the way an old smith looks at a young apprentice — with love, and a little impatience.

**Secret:** Ambri defeated Amirani in the epic — even dead. Amirani knows that Ambri is **still alive** in the grave, just as
he was alive in the barrow. At night Amirani sits by the grave and talks to Ambri. Sometimes the earth answers.

**Ambri's foot:** in the epic Amirani could not put the dead Ambri's foot back on the cart, and afterwards he sat in darkness, "day and night were one to him".
He has not forgotten that day. When the seal weakens, Amirani will be the first to go — and will once again fail to lift Ambri's burden (see the truth about King Aeetes XIV).
**The Bakbak-Devi:** in the epic Amirani has already killed the Bakbak-Devi once; from the devi's head three worms came out and turned into three dragons. Amirani killed two,
**the black one** got away. Amirani knows the devi is alive again — and so is the black dragon.

---

# The Infernal Legions

## Beelzebub, General of the Front

> "We will not attack tomorrow. We will not attack the day after. We will attack in a year, and that day they will be tired of waiting."
>
> — an order of Beelzebub's, intercepted by Iberian scouts

**One of the great princes of Hell.** General of the Caucasus front since 1907.

Beelzebub came to the front in 1907 and set up his headquarters on **the Grand Harness**. After that the war changed. The legions roar less and
wait more. Attacks come at exactly the right time. **The Winter of Wire** was his first plan.

Beelzebub does not go into battle. Almost no one has seen him. Heretics who serve at his headquarters say he sits at a great
table bearing a model of the front, and for days does not move a single piece. Then he moves one — and somewhere on the front hundreds
of people die.

He is courteous, cold and **never in a hurry**. He looks on the heretics with contempt, but never says so — he says "material".

**Secret:** Beelzebub **does not want** the seal broken — not yet. If the Father of Devis goes free, he will not submit to Hell. Beelzebub
is waiting for the moment when the seal breaks in exactly such a way that the Father of Devis becomes **Hell's captive**. That is why the Grand Harness is so slow.
The Harness-Lord does not know this.

---

## Marquis Sabnock

> "A fortress is a second armour. A wound is a second weapon."
>
> — a saying of Marquis Sabnock

**A marquis of Hell.** Field commander of the legions of the Wound.

The old lists say Marquis Sabnock **builds castles** and **makes wounds fester**. At the front they say both are true.
Every fortification inside the Wound was built by him — in a single night, by the hands of heretic workers. And every wound his
legionnaires inflict festers and does not heal — unless the Sisters of Medea arrive in time.

Sabnock stands at the front, with the legions. He is tall, clad in black armour and **lion-headed** — just as in the old lists.
He has **an old score** with Eristavi Zurab: in the Bloody Spring Zurab brought twelve captives out of his fortress.

**Secret:** Sabnock is fascinated by the **fortresses** of the surface — Georgian towers, seaside castles, trenches. What interests him is
how people build over centuries what demons can build in a single night. The captive smiths who
build his fortresses fear Sabnock less than other captives do.

---

# The Grand Harness

## The Harness-Lord

> "You ask me who I was. I was the one who listened. You did not listen — and that is why you will lose."
>
> — the Harness-Lord's words to the heretics, from an interrogation record

**Leader of the heretics.** One of the first leaders of the Listeners. No one knows his real name — the heretics call him
**the Harness-Lord**, lord of the Grand Harness. The brotherhood calls him "the one who left".

In 1838 a foreign mining company came to the foot of the Lesser Caucasus, and among its leaders was a man whose name
was written **differently every time** in the company's papers. When the Colchians blew up the Black Shaft in 1847, he escaped.

In 1914 this man is still alive. If he was a grown man in 1838, he is now over a hundred. He looks like a man of forty.

He speaks to the heretics **in many tongues**, and every heretic swears that the leader spoke to him in his mother tongue. Captives who have
seen him cannot describe his face — each describes it differently.

He is charismatic, warm and persuasive. He tells the heretics they are free. Many believe it.

**Secret:** the Harness-Lord does not want Hell to win. He wants **the Father of Devis** freed — and he believes the Father of Devis will break every
seal at once, Hell's too. He uses Beelzebub just as Beelzebub uses him. Each thinks the other does not realise.

---

## Rokapi

> "I left my chains in the underworld. The hearts I brought with me."
>
> — a song of the kudiani

**The ancient leader of the kudiani.** From folklore.

In folklore **Rokapi** is the leader of the kudiani — the hunchbacked, tailed witches who gather on the mountain. As a punishment she was chained
in the underworld, where she ate human hearts.

In 1871, in the great breakthrough, when the Lesser Caucasus opened, Rokapi's chains shattered. She came up out of the gate with the Father of Devis,
and the kudiani gathered around her again.

Rokapi lives on the Grand Harness, at the foot of the altar. The **Blood-Cupbearers** obey her. She is the one who leads the ritual —
and for every sacrifice she asks one thing: **the heart**.

**Secret:** Rokapi remembers well who chained her: **Kopala**. She thinks Kopala is on Khvamli, beside the chains. For Rokapi
the Grand Harness and the seal are secondary. She wants to climb Khvamli. By the old tradition the mountain opens **once every seven years**; the next
opening is **in 1919**. Rokapi is waiting for that day — and she knows that the two hundred who climbed in 1884 are still standing inside the mountain.

---

## The Bakbak-Devi

> "It raised its head and looked at the dragon. And the dragon, for the first time, fell back."
>
> — report of the Dragon's Field

**The mightiest of the devis.** From folklore.

In folklore the Bakbak-Devi is the strongest devi of all. After the great breakthrough, when Ambri sealed the gate, the Bakbak-Devi **remained on the surface** —
cut off from its father, the Father of Devis, who stayed below.

The heretics and the legions hunted it for **twenty-seven years**, found it, caught it and bound it in chains. Since 1899 it has been
**yoked at the head of the Grand Harness**, dragging the city. On the Dragon's Field (1904) the Dragon of the Fleece bit it in the throat. The wound does not heal.

The Bakbak-Devi is not the heretics' ally. It is their **captive**. They feed it, give it blood and tighten its chains. It is silent.

**Secret:** the Bakbak-Devi **is waiting**. It knows the Grand Harness is going to its father. When the city reaches Ambri's grave, the Bakbak-Devi
will break its chains — and its first victims will be **the heretics** who kept it in chains for twenty-seven years.
The second — **Amirani**: in the epic Amirani has already killed it once. A devi's heads grow back, and revenge even more so. The Bakbak-Devi
also knows that **the black dragon** — the worm that came out of its head and escaped Amirani — is waiting on the seabed.

---

## Open Questions
- ✅ Ambri's "silent word" — "lift" (see King Aeetes XIV).
- ✅ The fate of Eristavi Zurab's brother — alive, inside the Grand Harness (see Zurab).
- ✅ Who let the gas into the Iberian palace — the Voice-Master and the man who came out of Khvamli (see Armaz III).
- ✅ The dark side's game — now seven-sided, see `04-factions.md` ("the dark side's civil war").
- Who will lift Ambri's burden — the secret of the final campaign.

lore:07-gods.en:
The Gods and the Heavenly War

> Working version. The gods come from mythology and are used as mythology, not as religion.

---

## Two Wars

> "We think this war is ours. We are only its lower floor."
>
> — the words of Master Eldar

On the surface, people fight in the trenches. But that is **only part** of the war.

On the other side of the seals, where the human eye cannot reach, **the Heavenly War** is being fought. There Hell's **main legions** —
far greater than what has risen to the surface — fight **the Heavenly Host**: the gods and their winged warriors.

That is why the gods cannot help people directly:
- **The supreme gods** lead the Heavenly Host and cannot leave that war. If they are defeated there, Hell's main army
  will rise to the surface — and the trenches will not hold for a single day.
- **Some of the other gods** guard Amirani's chains on Khvamli.
- People were left only what the gods gave them in 1858: **the knowledge of the forge, the giants and alchemy**.

The legions that have risen to the surface are only Hell's **vanguard**. Even Beelzebub is a second-rank general in Hell's great war.

---

## The Supreme Gods

Every mythology has its own supreme god. All of them stand in one Heavenly Host, each with the gods of their own nation.

| Nation | Supreme god | What the myth says |
|---|---|---|
| **Colchis and Iberia** | **Armazi** | The supreme god of the pantheon of Kartli. Beside him: **Gatsi** (gold, on the right) and **Gaim** (silver, on the left) — "rulers of all secrets" |
| Armenia | **Aramazd** | The supreme god of the Armenian pantheon (the name is related to Armazi) |
| Hellenic League | **Zeus** | The vanquisher of the Titans |
| Rome | **Jupiter** | |
| Northern Union | **Odin** | |
| Slavic lands | **Perun** | The god of thunder |
| Celtic Isles | **The Dagda** | "The good god", who knows everything |
| Gaul | **Taranis** | |
| Finnish Forests | **Ukko** | The god of the sky and of thunder |
| Egypt | **Ra** | The sun god, whose barque fights Apep every night |
| Turkic peoples | **Tengri** / **Ülgen** | The god of the sky / Erlik's adversary |

⚠️ The highest figures of living religions (e.g. Amaterasu of Shinto) are not included here.

---

## Armazi

> "He won't come down. He stands above, at the very front, and where he stands, Hell cannot pass. That is enough."
>
> — the words of an Iberian mountain warden

**Armazi** is the highest of the Georgian gods. In the Heavenly Host he leads the Georgian gods — **Kopala** with his lightning, **Iakhsar**,
**the children of god** — and holds back one of Hell's great legions.

In the old days he had a **bronze idol** on a mountain near Mtskheta: a bronze man in a **golden chain shirt**, with a hard helmet,
**eyes of emerald and beryl**, a **sword** in his hand. To his right stood the golden idol of Gatsi, to his left the silver one of Gaim.

An old text says that Armazi **uses the sea as a weapon**.

### The Colossus of Armazi — Iberia's Giant

When the gods gave people the knowledge of the forge in 1858, the first thing the smiths of Iberia built was **the idol of Armazi** —
only this time **titan-sized** and alive.

**The Colossus of Armazi** — a bronze giant in a golden chain shirt, with eyes of emerald and beryl, with a sword — moves by steam and lightning.
It is not the god himself — it is the god's **statue**, holding part of the god's power. They say that when the colossus's emerald
eyes are alight, Armazi is watching from above.

On either side of the colossus walk two small giant-guardians: **golden Gatsi** and **silver Gaim**.

- **In the game:** the Colossus of Armazi is Iberia's **Tier V giant**.
- **Amirani** — the legendary titan-hero, Iberia's **special character** for special scenarios.

### Gatsi and Gaim — Patrons of Alchemy
The old texts say that Gatsi and Gaim ruled **"all secrets"**. Gold and silver are the two chief metals of alchemy.
That is why the Georgian alchemists — **the Sisters of Medea** in Colchis and **the Ekimbashi** in Iberia — trace their craft to the tradition of Gatsi and Gaim.

### Zaden — Fertility and Supply
**Zaden**, the god of fertility, was honoured with a colossus on Mount Zedazeni. In the war he is the patron of the front's **supply**: of the harvest, of food
and of the mountain springs from which **living** and **dead water** are drawn.

### Shavkhan and Pirkusha — the Georgian Smiths
Two Georgian smith deities give their names to the war's weapons: **Shavkhan** (Svan myth — forger of the heavenly chain and of the iron bridge over the abyss,
lame, like Hephaestus) is the patron of the smiths of Colchis, and **Pirkusha** (Pshav-Khevsur myth — the forger of Kopala's
weapons) of Iberia's thunderbolt weapons. Both are in the Heavenly Host and do not come down to the surface; their knowledge came in the gift of 1858.

### Ainina and Danina
Goddesses whose idols stood on the road to Mtskheta. In the war they are the patrons of **healing women**.

---

## The Heavenly Host

The Heavenly Host holds the gods of every mythology and their warriors — each under the banner of its own supreme god. They are not seen
on the surface. People know of them only by signs: lightning in a cloudless night sky, the sound of a bell in the mountains, the shadows of two armies in the sky
during an eclipse.

**The heavenly warriors** have no names. They are winged warriors, each in the tradition of its own mythology
(e.g. the riders of the Georgian gods, the warrior maidens of the Northern gods) — the heavenly mirror of Hell's legions.
Real religious names (archangels and others) are not used.

---

## Open Questions
- The battles of the Heavenly War — does anything happen that can be seen on the surface too?
- The name and appearance of the warriors of the Heavenly Host.
